prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

National Health Interview Survey
 

About NHIS

For Everyone
June 18, 2026

What to know

  • NHIS is the National Health Interview Survey.
  • NHIS is a national survey that monitors the health of the U.S. population.
  • NHIS statistics provide insights into the health of people of different ages, sexes, races and ethnicities, geographic locations, and social and economic circumstances.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of people across the country—the U.S. population—by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics. NHIS focuses on the health of U.S. children and adults.

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) conducts NHIS. It is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey. NHIS began collecting data in 1957.

Each year, NHIS collects data from about 27,000 adults through confidential, face-to-face interviews throughout the year. Many of these adults also provide health information about children in their households.

NHIS collects data from civilians who don't live in institutions. Civilians are people not serving on active duty in the military. Institutionalized people live in places like correctional facilities, skilled-nursing homes, and mental (psychiatric) hospitals.

NCHS is exploring new ways for you to participate in NHIS. Some people may receive a paper questionnaire while others will receive an invitation to complete the survey online. Some people may receive both. Your participation matters no matter how you complete the survey. If you need assistance with the survey or have questions, please call the number on the letter you received or email nhis@census.gov.

Selected to participate in the survey?

Learn why you should take part in NHIS and what to expect.
Visit our participant website

What's collected

NHIS collects data through personal interviews. One adult household member provides information about their own health and the health of others in their households.

NHIS collects data about health topics like—

  • Illness and chronic conditions
  • Injuries and chronic pain
  • Health-related behaviors
  • Ability to perform daily activities (functioning) and disability
  • Healthcare access and use
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Preventive services to identify and prevent health problems

The U.S. Census Bureau employs and trains field staff to conduct these interviews. They follow procedures developed by NCHS experts. Field staff conduct most interviews in person. Sometimes they conduct follow-up interviews over the phone.

Did you know?

NHIS content is updated about every 15–20 years to reflect advances in survey methodology and coverage of health topics. In 2019, NHIS launched redesigned content and structure that differs from the earlier questionnaire design (1997–2018).

Data and documentation

NCHS publishes reports featuring expert analysis of NHIS data. Selected estimates also are available as part of our interactive data query systems that provide tables and charts.

In producing these resources, NHIS staff prioritize protecting participants' privacy.

Data files

NHIS public use data files are available to download in multiple formats. All potentially identifiable information has been removed to ensure the confidentiality of participants and their households.

NHIS restricted data files are available through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center (RDC) for a fee. To access restricted NHIS data, researchers must submit requests in the Standard Application Process portal. The RDC provides instructions for preparing and submitting an application to access restricted data.

NHIS data also has been linked with data from other sources. This provides more robust datasets that can be used to analyze complex relationships between data from different sources. These linked datasets are available in the RDC.

Find data documentation for these datasets at Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation.

How the data are used

NCHS staff use NHIS data to produce official national health estimates. One of NHIS's key strengths is its ability to produce estimates for many subgroups of the U.S. population. NHIS can do this because it collects data from such a large group of people.

NHIS health statistics provide health information by—

  • Demographic characteristics, like age and marital status
  • Geographic location, like region and metro area size
  • Social and economic circumstances, like employment status and poverty level

These data help researchers, policymakers, and other data users better understand how health differs among these groups.

NHIS data drive policies and programs to improve health. NHIS results have helped track the health status of Americans, their access to health care, and the nation's progress toward achieving health goals.

Contact us

Email nhis@cdc.gov with any questions about the National Health Interview Survey.

NHIS-Teen

For Everyone
July 9, 2026

Key points

  • The National Health Interview Survey-Teen (NHIS-Teen) was an online survey of teenagers ages 12–17.
  • The survey gathered health information about teens from teens.
  • Data were collected from July 2021 to December 2023.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey-Teen (NHIS-Teen) was an online health survey of teenagers ages 12–17. Data were collected between July 2021 and December 2023. Health and survey experts from the academic research community and the federal government provided input to help the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) develop NHIS-Teen.

Invitations to participate in NHIS-Teen were sent to teenagers living in all 50 states and District of Columbia whose parent or guardian completed the NHIS Sample Child Interview and gave permission for their teenager to be invited.

Answers from parents and their children helped paint a picture of the health of teenagers living in the United States. Legislators, policymakers, and health organizations can use these data to better understand and serve the health needs of teenagers.

NHIS-Teen topics

NHIS-Teen covered questions on a variety of health topics, including—

  • Doctor visits
  • Sleep
  • Physical activity
  • Injuries
  • Mental health
  • Social and emotional support
  • Experiences with bullying and discrimination

NHIS-Teen data can be accessed only through the NCHS Research Data Center (RDC). There is no public-use NHIS-Teen file available.

Find more information about applying for access to NHIS-Teen data on the RDC Application Process web page. You can find variable names in the NHIS-Teen questionnaire.

Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

What to know

  • The National Center for Health Statistics conducted the Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander National Health Interview Survey (NHPI NHIS) in 2014.
  • The NHPI NHIS collected information about the health of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders in all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

Overview

The 2014 Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander National Health Interview Survey (NHPI NHIS) was the first federal survey designed to exclusively measure the health of Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander people. NHPI NHIS collected data from about 3,000 households with one or more NHPI residents.

The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) modeled the NHPI NHIS on the National Health Interview Survey.

Using the 2014 National Health Interview Survey, NCHS collected information for the NHPI NHIS about:

  • Health status and health conditions
  • Disability
  • Access to and use of health services
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Vaccinations
  • Health-related behaviors, like physical activity and sleep
  • Characteristics and behaviors that increase the risk of illness, injury, or death (risk factors)

Contact us‎

Email nhis@cdc.gov or call (301) 458-4901 for more information.

Collecting data

Trained U.S. Census Bureau NHIS interviewers used the 2014 NHIS questionnaires for NHPI NHIS. As a result, statistics from the 2014 NHPI NHIS can be compared to 2014 NHIS statistics

  • The Early Release Program provides data about health insurance coverage, wireless substitution, and several important health measures.
  • Access these data in tables, interactive data query systems, reports, and data files.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) Early Release program provides preliminary data much sooner than the final NHIS data files are ready for release. Preliminary estimates are available for insurance coverage, wireless phone substitution, and additional important health measures (key health indicators). Preliminary files of data at the individual participant level (microdata) on these topics are also available.

Restricted data

Researchers can access restricted NHIS variables for each Early Release through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center. They can also find information about NHIS restricted variables.

Questionnaire changes

NHIS launched a redesigned questionnaire in 2019. Following this redesign, some Early Release indicators have changed. Thus, the contents of preliminary microdata files from 2019 and later years are different from previous versions.

Preliminary microdata files are available for adults and children. The Early Release program includes two files for both groups—

  1. Information on wireless substitution
  2. Information on key health indicators and health insurance coverage

When data are available for both adults and children, you can join the adult file and child file together to calculate age estimates.

Users can view total national estimates and estimates by

PUBLIC-USE PAIR WEIGHTS DATA FROM THE NATIONAL HEALTH INTERVIEW SURVEY FILE DOCUMENTATION 
			(FOR USE IN THE PARENT-CHILD-PAIR LEVEL STATISTICAL ANALYSIS)
                                  

 
Backgroud: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) since 1957, 
is the principal source of information on the health of the civilian noninstitutionalized US population. The NHIS selects one 
adult (Sample Adult) and, when applicable, one child (Sample Child) randomly within a family (through 2018) or a household 
(2019 and forward). Sampling weights for the separate analysis of data from Sample Adults and Sample Children are provided 
annually by NCHS.There is growing interest in the analysis of parent-child pair data using NHIS, which necessitated the development 
of appropriate analytic weights. Since NHIS does not sample a parent-child pair from all possible parent-child pairs within a 
family or a household, the sampling weights for specific dyads (for example, father-child and mother-child) cannot be developed. 
However, sampling weights for adult-child pairs can be created more generally. Once adult-child pair sampling weights are created, 
domain estimation methods (that is, statistical analysis for subpopulations or subgroups) can produce estimates separately for 
mother-child and father-child pairs since mother-child and father-child pairs are a subset of all adult-child pairs. 
To meet the needs of data users, NCHS developed adult-child pair sampling weights for use in the analysis of mother-child 
and father-child pair data of NHIS (2019 and forward). This readme.txt file contains information on the public-use NHIS pair weights
data.

* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * ** * * * * * * * * * * *
The public-use pair weights data from different survey years have the same data structure. Each year’s pair weights are in a file that 
includes a household ID and the pair weights.
 
(1) File name: final_pair_weight&year.sas7bdat, where &year is the year of the NHIS survey. For example, final_pair_weight2019.sas7bdat
    is the file that contains the pair weights of the 2019 NHIS. 
(2) Variable names: HHX (household ID, for linking to Sample Adult and Sample Child data) and final_pair_weight (the pair weights).

* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * ** * * * * * * * * * * *
To use the public-use pair weights data

After linking the pair weights to Sample Adult and Sample Child datasets using HHX, users can derive mother-child/father-child/non-parent-child pairs 
using variables SAPARENTSC_A (Sample Adult relationship to Sample Child) and SEX_A (Sex of Sample Adult). These two variables are available in the Sample Adult public-use data files. 
The SAS code and a few analytical examples demonstrating how to conduct statistical analysis using the pair weights can be found in the NCHS report 
titled "Developing sampling weights for statistical analysis of parent-child pair data from the National Health Interview Survey", 
by Guangyu Zhang, Yulei He, Van Parsons, Chris Moriarity, Stephen Blumberg, Benjamin Zablotsky, Aaron Maitland, Matthew Bramlett, Jonaki Bose.  
 
The pair weights are for use in the analysis of NHIS mother-child or father-child pair data. These weights can be used when data from a mother 
(or father) are being incorporated in a child-level analysis as an exposure or independent variable, or if a joint child-mother/father outcome is 
being used in the analysis. The pair weights should not be used in the statistical analyses focusing exclusively on all Sample Adults (or all Sample Children); 
instead, the Sample Adult (or Sample Child) sampling weights developed by NCHS should be used for the corresponding analyses. 
For example, Sample Child sampling weights should be used for an analysis of a health outcome for children using data from all Sample Children 
(that is, including those whose families did not complete a Sample Adult interview). Although the Sample Adult (and Sample Child) sampling weights 
are correlated with the pair weights, pair-level statistical analyses should use the pair-level sampling weights as they incorporate the sampling probabilities
of both the Sample Adult and the Sample Child and are adjusted for pair-level nonresponse. Using Sample Adult weights or Sample Child weights for pair-level 
statistical analysis may lead to biased results.  
 
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * ** * * * * * * * * * * *
 
CAUTION - The SAS code in the NCHS report mentioned above uses the 2019 NHIS Sample Adult and Sample Child data for illustration. For NHIS data in different years, variable names may change. 
Users should check the log file if errors occur when applying the SAS code for different years of NHIS Sample Adult and Sample Child data. 
                                                                                                
   For questions, suggestions, or comments concerning NHIS pair weights data, please
   contact the Divsion of Health Interview Survey

2028 NHIS Questionnaire Redesign

For Everyone
Aug. 21, 2026

What to know

  • The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is proposing updates to the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).
  • NCHS is redesigning NHIS to modernize its data collection process.
  • The redesign is in response to rising costs, growing difficulty in reaching households, and the need for a more flexible and efficient survey.

Overview

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) has proposed a redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Since 1957, NHIS has collected and analyzed health data to monitor the health of people across the country.

The proposed NHIS redesign includes—

  • Revisions to the adult and child questionnaires
  • Use of a sequential mixed-mode data collection design with self-response options

Changes to the questionnaires are intended to improve the measurement of contemporary health topics and reduce respondent burden through shorter and less complex instruments.

The redesign reflects the ongoing need to maintain a gold-standard national health survey while adapting to increasing data collection costs and respondent preferences by incorporating lower-cost, self-administered data collection modes.

NHIS was previously redesigned in 1997 and 2019.

Proposed content

Review the draft questionnaires and a brief description of the redesign (in the Federal Register) to learn more—

  • Adult Questionnaire
  • Child Questionnaire
  • Federal Register Notice

Public comment

NCHS invites public comment on all areas of the proposed redesign. Comments are especially welcome regarding—

  • Structure, length, and clarity of the revised questionnaire
  • Shift to a sequential mixed mode design
  • Proposed addition or removal of content
  • How these changes may affect data quality, usability, and trends over time

Commenters who suggest questionnaire additions are encouraged to identify the minimum question sets to meet identified data needs.

NCHS is also interested in comments on the practical utility of child-level data collection that is largely limited to domains for which all-person population estimates are desired (i.e., population estimates that have historically relied on data from both the adult and child-focused interviews).

Questions?

Email healthsurveys@cdc.gov with any questions about the 2028 redesign.

Comment submission

Written comments must be received on or before October 20, 2026.

You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. CDC-2026-1387 by any of the following methods:

  • Federal eRulemaking Portal:
    • Go to the Federal Register Notice
    • Click on the blue "Comment" button at the top to submit comments
  • Mail: Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection Review Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road, N.E., MS-D74, Atlanta, Georgia 30329

[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 160 (Thursday, August 20, 2026)]
[Notices]
[Pages 53869-53871]
From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]
[FR Doc No: 2026-17040]



[[Page 53869]]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

[60Day-26-0214; Docket No. CDC-2026-1387]


Proposed Data Collection Submitted for Public Comment and 
Recommendations

AGENCY: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of 
Health and Human Services (HHS).

ACTION: Notice with comment period.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as part 
of its continuing effort to reduce public burden and maximize the 
utility of government information, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on a continuing 
information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 
1995. This notice invites comment on the National Health Interview 
Survey (NHIS). This Extension is designed to include the continuation 
of current questionnaire content and data collection operations in 
2027, as well as a systemic redesign of the NHIS to be implemented in 
2028.

DATES: Written comments must be received on or before October 19, 2026.

ADDRESSES: You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. CDC-2026-
1387 by either of the following methods:
     Federal eRulemaking Portal: www.regulations.gov. Follow 
the instructions for submitting comments.
     Mail: Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection Review 
Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road 
NE, MS H21-8, Atlanta, Georgia 30329.
    Instructions: All submissions received must include the agency name 
and Docket Number. CDC will post, without change, all relevant comments 
to www.regulations.gov.
    Please note: Submit all public comments through the Federal 
eRulemaking portal (www.regulations.gov) or by U.S. mail to the address 
listed above.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: To request more information on the 
proposed project or to obtain a copy of the information collection plan 
and instruments, contact Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection 
Review Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton 
Road NE, MS H21-8, Atlanta, Georgia 30329; Telephone: 404-639-7570; 
Email: [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 
(PRA) (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520), federal agencies must obtain approval from 
the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of 
information they conduct or sponsor. In addition, the PRA also requires 
federal agencies to provide a 60-day notice in the Federal Register 
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each new 
proposed collection, each proposed extension of existing collection of 
information, and each reinstatement of previously approved information 
collection before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To 
comply with this requirement, we are publishing this notice of a 
proposed data collection as described below.
    The OMB is particularly interested in comments that will help:
    1. Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is 
necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, 
including whether the information will have practical utility;
    2. Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of 
the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the 
methodology and assumptions used;
    3. Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to 
be collected;
    4. Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those 
who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, 
electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or 
other forms of information technology, e.g., permitting electronic 
submissions of responses; and
    5. Assess information collection costs.

Proposed Project

    National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) (OMB Control No. 0920-0214, 
Exp. 12/31/2026)--Revision--National Center for Health Statistics 
(NCHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Background and Brief Description

    Section 306 of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act (42 U.S.C.), as 
amended, authorizes that the Secretary of Health and Human Services 
(HHS), acting through NCHS, shall collect statistics on the extent and 
nature of illness and disability of the population of the United 
States. The annual National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is a major 
source of general statistics on the health of the U.S. population and 
has been in the field continuously since 1957. This voluntary and 
confidential household-based survey collects demographic and health-
related information from a nationally representative sample of 
households and noninstitutionalized, civilian persons throughout the 
country. NHIS data have long been used by government, academic, and 
private researchers to evaluate both general health and specific 
issues, such as smoking, diabetes, health care coverage, and access to 
health care. The survey is also a leading source of data for the 
Congressionally-mandated ``Health US'' and related publications, as 
well as the single most important source of statistics to track 
progress toward HHS health objectives.
    The current NHIS Sample Adult and Sample Child Questionnaires 
include annual core content that is scheduled to be fielded in the 
survey every year, rotating content that is fielded periodically, 
emerging content to address new topics of growing interest, and 
sponsored content that is fielded when external funding is available. 
Rotating Sample Adult and Sample Child core content on service 
utilization, physical activity (including walking for adults), and 
sleep that was on the NHIS in 2026 will rotate off in 2027. Content on 
alcohol use, fatigue, and smoking history and cessation will also 
rotate off the sample Adult Core, and content on height and weight, 
neighborhood characteristics, and screen time will rotate off the 
Sample Child core. The 2027 Sample Adult rotating core will include 
items on chronic conditions, allergies, and hearing and communication--
content previously fielded on the 2024 NHIS. It will also include 
content on preventative screening and aspirin use, and chronic pain, 
content that was previously fielded in 2025. Content on injuries and 
detailed employment information that was fielded on the 2026 Sample 
Adult survey will continue in 2027. The 2027 Sample Child content will 
include questions on injuries (continuing from 2026), allergies 
(previously fielded in 2024) and stressful life events (previously 
fielded in 2025).
    Sponsored content on complementary and integrative health, using 
questions similar to those previously fielded in 2022, will be included 
on both the 2027 Sample Adult and Sample Child Questionnaires. Sample 
Adult and Child Questionnaires for 2027 will also include vision and 
other difficulties with taste, smell, hearing and communication using 
similar questions to those fielded in 2023.
    Sponsored content from the 2026 Adult and Child Questionnaires on

[[Page 53870]]

chronic fatigue will remain in 2027. Sponsored content from the 2026 
Adult Questionnaire on life satisfaction, diabetes, social support, 
loneliness, and isolation, tobacco product use, chronic fatigue, 
immunizations, whole person health, and social functioning and age of 
disability onset will also remain. Sponsored content on the 2027 Adult 
Questionnaire will also include questions on cancer screening, 
caregiving, epilepsy, and psoriasis, similar to questions previously 
fielded in 2025, and questions on occupational health, psoriasis and 
Crohn's/ulcerative colitis, similar to questions fielded in 2023 and 
2024.
    Like in past years, and in accordance with the 1995 initiative to 
increase the integration of surveys within the HHS, respondents to the 
2027 NHIS will serve as the sampling frame for the Medical Expenditure 
Panel Survey conducted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and 
Quality (AHRQ). A subsample of NHIS respondents and/or members of 
commercial survey panels may be identified to participate in short 
methodological and cognitive testing activities to evaluate the 
questionnaire and/or inform work to redesign the data collection 
methods and questionnaires for 2028. In addition, subsamples of NHIS 
respondents may be recontacted by web, phone, or mail to ask follow-up 
questions on topics that are already included in the NHIS. The NHIS 
also includes content that is used to benchmark estimates and calibrate 
survey weights from probability-based online commercial survey panels 
as part of the NCHS Rapid Surveys System.
    To maintain data quality and contain operational costs, a redesign 
of the NHIS is being planned for implementation in 2028. The redesigned 
NHIS will expand upon the strengths of the current in-person data 
collection methodology by incorporating lower-cost, self-administered 
data collection modes to account for respondent preferences and reduce 
operational costs. This will be done using a sequential mixed-mode data 
collection approach in which sampled households are first invited to 
respond using self-administered online and paper questionnaires. Census 
Bureau field representatives will then conduct in-person follow-up for 
some households that do not respond to self-response modes, preserving 
the long-standing quality standards of the NHIS while modernizing its 
operational model. This mixed-mode design will be refined through a 
series of cognitive, usability, and field tests. This redesign of both 
survey operations and questionnaire content is strategically timed to 
coordinate with the data cycle used to monitor Healthy People 2030 
objectives, providing a timely transition into the next decade of 
monitoring the nation's critical public health indicators. It is also 
timed to coincide with the Census Bureau's deployment of its new 
modernized data collection program--Data Ingest and Collection for the 
Enterprise (DICE)--that will improve the NHIS's ability to collect data 
from respondents through paper, internet, and interviewer-assisted 
modes.
    The redesigned 2028 NHIS will continue to include an Adult 
Questionnaire completed by one randomly selected adult aged 18 or older 
in each sampled household. Consistent with current practices, 
information about the selected adult will be collected from the adult 
himself/herself unless s/he is physically or mentally unable to do so, 
in which case a knowledgeable proxy will be allowed to answer for the 
adult. The redesigned 2028 NHIS will also continue to include questions 
regarding one randomly selected child under age 18 in each household 
with children. Information about the child will be collected from a 
parent or guardian living with the child. Draft questionnaires for both 
adults and children have been included in this docket for public review 
and comment. The draft 2028 questionnaires can also be viewed on the 
NHIS website at https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/2028-questionnaire-redesign.html. It is expected that these questionnaires will be revised 
following the public comment period.
    The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is particularly 
interested in comments that support the planning of the redesign to be 
implemented in 2028. Comments are especially welcome regarding the 
structure, length, and clarity of the redesigned adult and child 
questionnaires; the implications of adopting a sequential mixed-mode 
design; the importance of specific content additions or removals; and 
the potential effect of these changes on data quality, usability, and 
trend measurement. Commenters who suggest questionnaire additions are 
encouraged to identify the minimum question sets to meet identified 
data needs. NCHS is also interested in comments on the practical 
utility of child-level data collection that is largely limited to 
domains for which all-person population estimates are desired (i.e., 
population estimates that have historically relied on data from both 
the adult and child-focused interviews).
    The redesigned questionnaires will retain key health measures that 
are essential for tracking public health trends. Key health measures in 
the draft adult questionnaire include longstanding items on major 
chronic health conditions, foundational measures of disability and 
functional status based on the Washington Group Short Set, and key 
measures of health insurance coverage, continuity, and adequacy. Topic 
areas in this draft questionnaire also include healthcare utilization, 
access to care, medication use, and prescription nonadherence. 
Behavioral and demographic covariates are also included. The draft 
adult questionnaire introduces several new content areas to reflect 
contemporary health information needs. These include a recently 
validated summary measure of overall health and well-being known as the 
Whole Person Health Index and new questions on high-deductible health 
plans, insurance adequacy, primary care, asthma treatment, and 
marijuana use.
    Because the redesigned NHIS will include self-administered online 
and mailed questionnaires, the redesigned 2028 questionnaire will 
necessarily be shorter in length and less complicated in structure, as 
compared to the current questionnaire. Many of the more detailed 
questions on particular topics that were fielded annually from 2019 to 
2027 are not included in the draft adult questionnaire for 2028. Also, 
the redesigned NHIS questionnaire structure does not include a detailed 
schedule of content that rotates on and off the survey with a set 
periodicity established years in advance. This change is necessary to 
both shorten the questionnaire and to preserve an agile and dynamic 
design that allows for the addition of content on topics of current and 
emerging interest. Space will still be reserved for federal agencies to 
fund sponsored content. For example, in 2028, NCHS anticipates 
including sponsored content on screening for breast, cervical, and 
colorectal cancer and on injury, among others.
    OMB Clearance is sought for three years, to collect data for 2027-
2029. For 2027 data collection, the docket includes detailed 
descriptions of sampling, questionnaires, data collection procedures, 
and other survey design components. These details have not yet been 
finalized for the 2028 and 2029 data collections. Therefore, the plans 
for the updated survey design are described only at a high level in 
this package. NCHS will submit more details regarding 2028 data 
collection, including revised questionnaires, to the Office of 
Management and Budget for approval in 2027.

# National Health Interview Survey: research and preservation report

**Research checked:** October 8, 2026  
**Official publisher:** National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)  
**Official homepage:** https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

## Executive summary

The **National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)** is a foundational federal statistical program measuring the health of the U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized population. It began interviewing households in **July 1957**, following the **National Health Survey Act of 1956**. NCHS designs, processes, analyzes, and publishes the survey; the **U.S. Census Bureau collects the interview data on NCHS’s behalf**.

NHIS is better understood as a **continuing survey program and a family of annual datasets**, not a single file. Its products include adult and child microdata, questionnaires, codebooks, income imputations, survey-methodology documentation, special analytical weights, preliminary estimates, official reports, and restricted linked datasets.

Its principal public value is that it measures health **outside the healthcare system**: people without insurance, people who cannot afford care, and people with conditions or limitations that may never appear in medical claims. It supports national health surveillance, health-equity research, policy evaluation, and monitoring of federal health objectives.

For preservation and analysis, four cautions are especially important:

1. **Collection began in 1957, but available historical microdata begin in 1963.**
2. **The 2019 redesign created a substantial break in comparability.**
3. **Pandemic-era procedures and the 2025 interruption in collection require year-specific treatment.**
4. **Public-use files are freely accessible but remain subject to statutory confidentiality and data-use restrictions.**

The latest complete annual public-use release identified during this research is **survey year 2025, released in 2026**. CDC is also proposing a major mixed-mode redesign for **2028**.

## 3. Who produces it, and under what authority?

### Institutional responsibilities

**NCHS** is responsible for the statistical program: survey content and methods, processing, disclosure protection, weighting, documentation, official estimates, and dissemination.

The **Census Bureau** is the collection agent. It employs and trains field representatives, recruits selected households, and administers the survey using procedures developed for NHIS.

Other federal agencies can support **sponsored content**, allowing NHIS to answer specialized health-policy questions without creating a completely separate national survey. Sponsorship and question availability should be documented year by year.

### Statutory origin and continuing mandate

The **National Health Survey Act, Public Law 84-652, enacted July 3, 1956**, called for a continuing survey and special studies of the nation’s health, methodological research, and dissemination of results.

The principal current authorizing citation is:

- **Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act**
- **42 U.S.C. § 242k**

This establishes NCHS’s broader mandate to conduct and support statistical and epidemiological activities and collect statistics on health, illness, disability, and health services.

The Census Bureau conducts NHIS for NCHS under **13 U.S.C. § 8(b)**.

Source: [NCHS legislative authorities](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/misc/legislation2014.pdf), [Census legal-authority explanation](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nhis.html).

### Authorization is not compulsory participation

NHIS participation is **voluntary**. Its legal authorization should not be confused with a requirement that selected households answer.

### Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

NHIS operates under **OMB Control No. 0920-0214**. Federal information collections require OMB approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act and public notices addressing burden, necessity, and practical utility.

The August 20, 2026 notice identifies NHIS as a revision of an existing approved collection, with the then-current approval expiring December 31, 2026. **An approval expiration date is not itself evidence that the survey will end**; renewals and revisions are part of ordinary oversight.

Source: [Federal Register notice, August 20, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

### Funding and operational dependencies

NHIS depends on federal appropriations, NCHS program support, Census collection capacity, and funding for sponsored content. Its statutory mandate does not guarantee uninterrupted fieldwork or a fixed sample size.

This research did **not** establish a reliable current NHIS-only annual operating-budget figure. NCHS-wide budget totals should not be presented as the survey’s budget.

### The early-data preservation gap

CDC’s historical account states that **no microdata files exist before 1963**, although early questionnaires and statistical reports survive.

Therefore, preserving the earliest NHIS record requires preserving **published tables, reports, questionnaires, and methodological publications**, not merely collecting downloadable data files.

### The 2019 redesign

Before 2019, the survey collected information about all family members and selected an adult and child **per family** for more detailed interviews. From 2019 forward, it selects an adult and child **per household** and no longer publicly releases the same whole-household information.

Other changes included question wording, content periodicity, weighting, and race/ethnicity measurement.

IPUMS NHIS’s assessment of the bridge test recommends **not comparing pre-2019 and post-2019 trends as though they were one uninterrupted series**. Harmonizing variable codes does not eliminate changes in measurement or survey procedures.

Sources: [IPUMS redesign guidance](https://nhis.ipums.org/nhis/userNotes_2019_NHIS_Redesign.shtml), [bridge-test guidance](https://nhis.ipums.org/nhis/userNotes_bridge_test.shtml).

## 5. How the survey works

### Population coverage and exclusions

NHIS covers civilian, noninstitutionalized residents of the 50 states and DC. Current methodological documentation lists exclusions including:

- Active-duty military personnel;
- Civilians living on military bases;
- People in long-term-care institutions;
- People in correctional facilities;
- People without a fixed household address.

U.S. territories are outside the stated geographic target.

**Policy implication:** NHIS estimates should not be labeled as covering “everyone in America.” Its exclusions are particularly consequential in research about homelessness, incarceration, institutional disability, and long-term care.

### Probability sampling

NHIS uses geographically clustered, stratified probability sampling rather than convenience recruitment.

Beginning in 2025, the modified design uses **two stages**:

1. Selection of primary sampling units;
2. Annual selection of household units within those units.

Commercial address lists form the main address source, supplemented by field listing in selected areas. Sample designs are periodically updated following decennial censuses.

Source: [2025 complex-survey reporting checklist](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/2025-NHIS-PRICSSA-508.pdf).

### Interviewing

The principal mode is **computer-assisted personal interviewing**, typically initiated at the household, with telephone interviewing used as needed or requested.

The selected adult generally answers for themselves. A parent or knowledgeable responsible adult answers for the selected child. Adult self-report and child proxy-report are therefore different forms of measurement.

The selected adult and selected child are **not necessarily parent and child**, and in a multifamily household may not belong to the same family.

### Collection and release cycle

NHIS normally spreads interviewing across the year, helping capture seasonal variation. Final annual files follow processing, editing, weighting, and confidentiality review.

The Early Release Program publishes selected estimates sooner. Preliminary products may use different processing or weights and should not be silently substituted for final releases.

## 7. What information does NHIS contain?

NHIS combines health outcomes, healthcare access, behaviors, and social circumstances. Depending on year and module, topics include:

- **Health status and conditions:** general health, asthma, diabetes, cardiovascular conditions, cancer history, pain, fatigue, and other conditions;
- **Functioning and disability:** sensory, cognitive, mobility, daily-activity, and related limitations;
- **Mental health:** symptoms, distress, treatment, counseling, and related measures;
- **Health behaviors:** tobacco use, physical activity, sleep, and other behaviors;
- **Insurance:** coverage status, coverage type, and continuity;
- **Access to care:** usual source of care, affordability, delayed care, unmet need, and prescription-related barriers;
- **Healthcare use:** visits, hospital care, emergency care, and other services;
- **Prevention:** screening, vaccinations, and preventive services;
- **Child health:** conditions, developmental and functional measures, care access, and family circumstances;
- **Demographic and socioeconomic characteristics:** age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, education, employment, family income, and poverty measures;
- **Telephone status:** wireless-only and related household communication measures.

Not every topic appears every year or in both age groups. Since 2019, content has included:

1. Annual core content;
2. Rotating core content;
3. Sponsored content;
4. Emerging content.

**For librarians and analysts:** Preserve the questionnaire and content schedule with each year. A variable absent from a release may reflect planned rotation, discontinuation, restriction, or a different question universe—not ordinary missing data.

Source: [CDC overview](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/index.html), [2025 questionnaires and documentation](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/2025-nhis.html).

## 9. What data scientists need to know

### Use the survey design, not ordinary row-count statistics

For current adult and child files, key variables include:

- Adult weight: **`WTFA_A`**
- Child weight: **`WTFA_C`**
- Public-use stratum: **`PSTRAT`**
- Public-use primary sampling unit: **`PPSU`**

Weights support population estimates. Strata and PSU variables support appropriate uncertainty estimation.

A simple unweighted mean describes the responding sample, not necessarily the target population. Standard errors assuming independent, equally selected observations are generally inappropriate.

NCHS provides examples for SAS, SUDAAN, Stata, SPSS, and R. Source: [2025 reporting checklist](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/2025-NHIS-PRICSSA-508.pdf).

### Respect question universes and coded missingness

Distinguish:

- “No”;
- “Don’t know”;
- Refusal;
- Not ascertained;
- Not applicable;
- Not asked because of age, prior answers, or content rotation.

Special numeric codes must be interpreted from the codebook before analysis. Otherwise, they can be mistaken for valid measurements.

### Income requires multiple-imputation methods

Beginning in 2019, NHIS produces **10 imputed income values**; earlier modern releases used five.

Analyze all imputations and combine estimates and uncertainty using appropriate multiple-imputation procedures. Do not average the imputed values into one income value and treat it as observed, or stack imputations as if they were additional people.

Source: [2025 income-imputation technical document](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_Statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/NHIS2025-imputation-techdoc-508.pdf).

### Joint adult–child analysis needs special weights

Matching adult and child files on household identifier does not make the selected adult the child’s parent.

NCHS provides **`final_pair_weight`**, linked using **`HHX`**, for pair-level analyses. The adult relationship to the child can be identified using the appropriate relationship variables.

Ordinary adult or child weights may bias pair-level estimates because they do not account for the pair’s joint selection and response.

Source: [pair-weight README](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/nhis/2025/NHIS-PairWeights-README.txt).

### Pool years carefully

Before combining years:

- Verify question wording, universes, and response categories;
- Check sample-design and variance-variable instructions;
- Follow NCHS guidance on pooled weights;
- Preserve survey year in record identifiers;
- Account for rotating or partial-year content;
- Define whether the estimate represents an average annual population or another estimand.

Dividing weights by the number of years is not a universally sufficient solution.

### Handle 2020 as an exceptional release

The 2020 survey included:

- A Sample Adult file for single-year estimates;
- A longitudinal file connecting repeat interviews in 2019 and 2020;
- A partial file for certain multi-year analyses.

NHIS completed **10,415 followback interviews** with adults interviewed in 2019. This is an exception to its usual repeated-cross-sectional design.

Source: [2020 documentation](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/2020-nhis.html).

### Interpret models appropriately

NHIS can support descriptive and associational research, but cross-sectional associations do not establish causation.

For machine learning, analysts should additionally consider:

- Survey-weighted evaluation;
- Cluster-aware splitting where appropriate;
- Leakage from derived variables;
- Performance across demographic subgroups;
- Generalizability beyond the survey’s covered population.

The public-use files are not a clinical diagnostic dataset or a basis for identifying individual respondents.

## 10. Quality, limitations, and interpretive risks

### Nonresponse

Recent response rates are much lower than historical rates. Weighting can reduce nonresponse bias but cannot guarantee its elimination.

The 2025 adult and child weighted rates—approximately 41% and 42%—make sensitivity to nonresponse particularly important. Nevertheless, **response rate alone does not quantify bias**; the relationship between response propensity and the outcome matters.

### Self-report and proxy-report

Reported diagnoses depend partly on access to diagnosis. Healthcare visits and behaviors depend on recall. Sensitive answers can be affected by social desirability and interview mode.

Child proxy reports may differ from children’s own perceptions, especially for mental health and social experiences.

### Mode effects

In-person, telephone, paper, and online responses can differ because of both respondent composition and how questions are answered. Pandemic-era shifts and future self-response modes require evaluation rather than an assumption of equivalence.

### Confidentiality transformations

Public-use files omit or reduce identifying detail. Grouping, top-coding, suppression, and restrictions can limit analysis of exact ages, income extremes, small populations, and local conditions.

### Small subgroups

A large national sample does not ensure precise estimates for every intersection of age, race, disability, geography, and income. Analysts should report uncertainty and follow applicable NCHS presentation standards.

### Geography

NHIS is primarily designed for national health estimation. Restricted geographic access does **not** automatically make every state, county, or neighborhood estimate statistically reliable.

### Comparisons with other surveys

NHIS, NHANES, BRFSS, ACS, CPS, and MEPS differ in population coverage, mode, reference periods, wording, and purpose. Apparent discrepancies may be methodological rather than errors.

For example, NHIS is an interview survey, whereas NHANES includes examinations and laboratory measurements. Their disease measures are not interchangeable.

## 11. Typical users and benefits to the public

Federal notices explicitly identify government, academic, and private researchers as longstanding NHIS users. CDC identifies researchers and policymakers more broadly.

| User community | Typical applications |
|---|---|
| **HHS, CDC, and other federal agencies** | National surveillance, health-objective monitoring, program planning |
| **Public-health and health-services researchers** | Conditions, disability, behaviors, care access, and disparities |
| **Economists and policy analysts** | Insurance coverage, affordability, employment and health, policy evaluation |
| **State and local health organizations** | National benchmarks and subgroup context |
| **Advocacy and community organizations** | Evidence on unmet need, inequity, disability, and affordability |
| **Journalists and the public** | Interpreting changes in national health |
| **Survey methodologists** | Nonresponse, weighting, mode, measurement, and paradata research |
| **Educators and students** | Complex-survey training and reproducible analysis |

### Major public benefits

**1. Measuring people not visible in healthcare records.**  
Claims data describe insured people receiving billable care. NHIS also measures lack of coverage, delayed care, and unmet need.

**2. Connecting health to social circumstances.**  
It supports analysis by age, race and ethnicity, disability, employment, income, and other characteristics.

**3. Monitoring national goals.**  
NHIS is a major source for **Healthy People** monitoring and the congressionally mandated **Health, United States** reporting program.

**4. Evaluating policy.**  
Insurance and access measures can support assessment of reforms, although causal conclusions require a defensible design.

**5. Understanding prevention gaps.**  
Screening and behavioral measures help identify where prevention and care access are falling short.

**6. Extending the value of other evidence.**  
Administrative linkages allow investigation of mortality, program participation, and healthcare use after interview.

**7. Supporting other survey methods.**  
Wireless-substitution statistics inform understanding of telephone-survey coverage.

These are documented or well-supported uses; they should not be read as evidence that NHIS alone caused a particular policy change.

## 12. Restricted data, linkages, and related surveys

### Research Data Center access

Sensitive NHIS variables and detailed geography require an approved project through the **NCHS Research Data Center (RDC)**. CDC currently directs applicants to the Standard Application Process portal at **ResearchDataGov.org**. Fees apply.

Researchers should budget for approval, access, and disclosure review. Restricted access is not equivalent to receiving unrestricted downloadable files.

Source: [restricted NHIS data](https://www.cdc.gov/rdc/restricted-nchs-variables/nhis.html).

### Linked datasets

NHIS has been linked to:

- National Death Index mortality records;
- Medicare and Medicaid records;
- HUD records;
- Medical Expenditure Panel Survey linkage products.

Access, years, eligibility, and weights vary by linkage.

**Important exception:** Some linked mortality data are public-use. Not all NHIS linkages are restricted.

At the time checked, CDC distinguished:

- **2019 public-use mortality linkage:** NHIS 1986–2018, limited adult mortality information;
- **2022 restricted-use mortality linkage:** NHIS 1986–2021, follow-up through December 31, 2022, with more detailed information.

A linkage’s release label is not necessarily its survey-year coverage.

Sources: [linked-data access](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/linked-data/about-access/index.html), [mortality linkage documentation](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/linked-data/mortality-files/index.html).

### NHIS-Teen

NHIS-Teen was an online survey of **ages 12–17**, conducted **July 2021–December 2023**, following parental permission after the main Sample Child interview.

It collected teens’ own reports on sleep, physical activity, mental health, social support, bullying, discrimination, and other topics.

**No public-use NHIS-Teen microdata file is available.** Microdata require RDC access; public dashboards and reports are available.

Source: [NHIS-Teen](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/teen/index.html).

### Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

The **2014 NHPI NHIS** was a separate survey designed specifically to measure Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander health. It covered about **3,000 households** and used the 2014 NHIS questionnaires.

It should be cataloged as a related, distinct resource, not silently combined with the regular annual sample.

Source: [NHPI NHIS](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/nhpi/index.html).

## 13. Confidentiality, rights, and permitted reuse

### Legal protections

Key protections include:

- **Public Health Service Act § 308(d), 42 U.S.C. § 242m(d);**
- **CIPSEA, 44 U.S.C. §§ 3561–3583;**
- **Privacy Act of 1974, 5 U.S.C. § 552a.**

Identifiable information is protected, and authorized staff and agents are subject to confidentiality obligations. Willful unlawful disclosure can carry serious criminal penalties.

### Public access is not unrestricted use

The NCHS Data User Agreement requires users to:

1. Use data for statistical reporting and analysis only;
2. Make no attempt to identify a person or establishment;
3. Not link files to individually identifiable data;
4. Not conduct prohibited re-identification or disclosure-method assessment activities.

Using the data signifies agreement to these requirements.

**Preservation implication:** Preserve and distribute the applicable data-use terms alongside the files. Do not label the resource “unrestricted” merely because it can be downloaded without an account.

Source: [NCHS Data User Agreement](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/policy/data-user-agreement.html).

### Citation and attribution

NCHS requests acknowledgment of the full source name:

> Data Source: National Center for Health Statistics, National Health Interview Survey, 2025.

The 2025 suggested dataset citation is:

> National Center for Health Statistics. National Health Interview Survey, 2025. Public-use data file and documentation. 2026.

For reproducibility, add the specific file, release/version, URL, and access date. NCHS also asks authors to distinguish their own interpretations and conclusions from those of the agency.

NHIS questionnaires are expressly identified as **public domain**, with source citation appreciated.

Source: [2025 survey description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/srvydesc-508.pdf).

## 14. Preservation strategy

The following are **recommended preservation practices**, not claims that CDC currently implements every item.

### Preserve a release package, not just a CSV

For each survey year, preserve:

- Original compressed data;
- Extracted files;
- All codebooks, layouts, and import programs;
- Questionnaires and field manuals;
- Survey descriptions and weighting guidance;
- Income imputations and their documentation;
- Pair weights and special-file guidance;
- Correction notices;
- Data-use terms;
- Official tables and reports;
- Release webpages and their links.

### Keep originals and derivatives separate

Retain byte-identical agency originals. Store converted formats—such as Parquet or labeled statistical datasets—as derivatives with documented transformation code.

CSV alone does not preserve labels, question universes, special missing-value meanings, or survey-design semantics.

### Record provenance and fixity

Maintain a manifest including:

- Original URL and retrieval date;
- Survey and release year;
- File/document version;
- File size and record count;
- Cryptographic checksum, such as SHA-256;
- Original versus derived status;
- Access classification;
- Relationships between files;
- Revision history.

Use agency integrity metadata where available, and independently verify downloaded contents.

### Preserve changing web content

An HTML capture of a dashboard may not preserve its underlying estimates or interactive functions. Preserve downloadable tables, methods, available underlying data, and the query settings used.

CDC’s current and archived NHIS pages both contain historically valuable material. Capture linked documentation rather than assuming it will remain available at the same URL.

### Preserve analytical dependencies

Record software versions, recodes, pooling rules, age-standardization methods, uncertainty calculations, and suppression rules for derived estimates.

For IPUMS extracts, retain the extract definition and original-variable concordance.

### Respect restricted-data boundaries

Do not attempt to mirror confidential microdata or bypass RDC controls. Preservation of restricted resources should occur through authorized custodial arrangements.

A public repository can preserve restricted-file metadata and public documentation without holding the confidential records.

### Avoid unsupported archival claims

This research did not verify a specific NARA accession, NHIS records-retention schedule, or permanent-retention commitment for every component. Continued online availability is not itself proof of an archival guarantee.

## 15. Current issues for policy activists and preservationists

### Proposed 2028 redesign

CDC proposes:

- Revised adult and child questionnaires;
- Shorter, less complex instruments;
- Sequential mixed-mode collection;
- Self-response options.

The Federal Register description anticipates initial online and paper invitations, followed by in-person follow-up for some nonresponding households.

Potential benefits include lower costs, reduced burden, and better accommodation of respondent preferences. Potential risks include mode effects, reduced topical detail, changed population coverage, and disrupted trends.

**These remain proposals, not finalized 2028 specifications.**

Sources: [CDC redesign page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/2028-questionnaire-redesign.html), [Federal Register description](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

### Public participation opportunity

As of this research date, CDC’s redesign page states:

- **Docket:** CDC-2026-1387
- **Comment deadline:** October 20, 2026
- **Submission page:** [Regulations.gov notice](https://www.regulations.gov/document/CDC-2026-1387-0001)
- **Redesign questions:** healthsurveys@cdc.gov

CDC particularly welcomes comments on content additions/removals, questionnaire clarity, mixed-mode collection, and effects on data quality and trends.

### Useful accountability questions

Researchers and advocates may wish to ask:

- Which measures will cease to be annual?
- What bridge studies will quantify redesign effects?
- How will mode-specific bias be evaluated?
- How will people with limited internet access or accessibility needs be reached?
- Will shortened child content still support child-specific policy needs?
- Will retired variables, draft questionnaires, tests, and correction histories remain preserved?
- How will subgroup precision and restricted-data access be maintained?
- How will collection interruptions and operational constraints be documented?

These questions address statistical continuity and public access without presuming that modernization is inherently harmful.

## 16. Bottom-line assessment

**NHIS is a high-priority preservation resource.** It is a long-running national record of health, disability, behavior, insurance, and unmet healthcare need, with substantial scientific and civic value.

Its greatest strengths are broad topical coverage, probability sampling, inclusion of people outside healthcare records, extensive documentation, and administrative-linkage possibilities.

Its greatest vulnerabilities are nonresponse, population exclusions, changing modes and questions, confidentiality-related loss of detail, operational interruptions, and major redesign breaks.

The central practical recommendation is:

> **Preserve NHIS as a documented statistical system—not merely as annual rows of data.**

Without its questionnaires, universes, weights, codebooks, revisions, and collection history, the files can remain readable while becoming analytically misleading.

# NHIS dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 8, 2026**  
**Dataset:** National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)  
**Primary publisher:** CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), with collection by the U.S. Census Bureau

## Overall finding

**NHIS remains an operating, publicly accessible survey, but several risks have already materialized.** These include policy-directed removal of gender-identity questions, withholding of previously collected gender-identity data, interrupted collection in 2025, reduced temporal detail in published products, and substantial disruption at its parent agency.

The evidence is stronger for **loss of particular variables, coverage, and analytical continuity** than for imminent disappearance of the entire historical archive. Public-use copies distributed through resources such as IPUMS provide some protection for already-released information, but cannot replace unpublished variables or observations never collected.

**Important update to my preceding report:** Additional research identified a significant omission: NCHS explicitly states that gender-identity information collected in 2024 is unavailable **both in public-use files and through the Research Data Center**, and that collection was discontinued in 2025.

### Assessment conventions

- These are **rubric classifications, not numerical probabilities**.
- I distinguish implemented changes from proposals and enacted appropriations from budget requests.
- The staffing rating includes **CDC-level dependencies**, while separately identifying NCHS-specific evidence.
- This is a documentary assessment, **not a complete file-by-file or checksum comparison of historical releases**.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

**Moderate Risk — evidence supporting element-level loss or exclusion**

- The official **2024 NHIS Survey Description** identifies gender identity as collected emerging content, but states:

  > “These data are not available in the public-use file or through the Research Data Center.”

  The same footnote references Executive Order 14168 and discontinuation of collection in the 2025 NHIS. This establishes an access gap for a data element collected in a completed historical survey year—not merely a proposal to stop future collection.  
  Source: [NCHS, 2024 Survey Description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2024/srvydesc-508.pdf).

**No Known Issue — evidence supporting continued availability of most historical files**

- CDC’s documentation portal continues to list annual resources for **2019–2025** and directs users to CDC Archive resources for **1997–2018 and earlier years**. There is no evidence here that whole historical annual NHIS releases have broadly disappeared.  
  Source: [NHIS documentation portal](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/index.html).
- Independent redistribution and harmonization through [IPUMS NHIS](https://nhis.ipums.org/nhis-action/faq) provide an additional access path for incorporated public-use variables.

**High Risk / Gone — not established**

- I did not establish removal of entire historical annual data files sufficient for either rating.
- General CDC website removals in early 2025 demonstrate institutional vulnerability, but are not proof that specific NHIS annual files remain missing.  
  Context: [NPR, February 6, 2025](https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/02/06/nx-s1-5288113/cdc-website-health-data-trump).

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

Historical files generally remain accessible, but a collected historical data element is explicitly unavailable through either public or approved restricted access.

**Interpretive qualification:** I found evidence of **withholding/exclusion**, not proof that the 2024 gender-identity variables were once publicly downloadable and then deleted. If this category is limited strictly to alteration of *previously distributed public-use files*, the defensible rating would instead be **No Known Issue**, with this withholding recorded separately. I use Moderate Risk because your wording encompasses historical data elements that exist in the dataset but are removed from accessible products.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

**High Risk — partial collection/publication omission**

- NCHS’s final 2025 documentation reports that collection paused between **October 1 and November 16, 2025**, following the lapse in appropriations.
- October and November sample interviewing was delayed. The **December sample was interviewed in January 2026 and excluded from the 2025 annual files**.
- Consequently, the 2025 annual files contain **11 months of sample**, with weights adjusted accordingly. This is an actual omission from the annual release, not merely an anticipated risk.  
  Source: [NCHS, 2025 Survey Description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/srvydesc-508.pdf).

**Moderate Risk — confirmed delays**

- The same documentation reports “slight delays” in processing and shifted interviewing periods. These independently satisfy the rubric’s delayed-collection criterion.
- Adjusting weights mitigates estimation problems but does not restore the original collection calendar or the missing annual-file sample.

**No Known Issue — continuing authorization and publication**

- Final 2025 public-use files and documentation are available.  
  Source: [2025 NHIS release page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/2025-nhis.html).
- The August 2026 Federal Register notice identifies **OMB Control No. 0920-0214**, expiring **December 31, 2026**, and seeks clearance for **2027–2029**. At this assessment date, the documented approval has not expired. The notice is evidence of renewal activity, **not proof of completed renewal**.  
  Source: [Federal Register notice, official GovInfo copy](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-20/html/2026-17040.htm).

**Gone — not supported**

- Neither collection nor publication has been terminated.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Under the rubric’s “collection or publication skipped” language, the omission of one monthly sample from the annual files warrants High Risk.

**Qualification:** No entire annual NHIS cycle was canceled. If “skipped” means only a whole annual cycle, this would be **Moderate Risk** instead. The rating should not be interpreted as evidence that NHIS itself has ended.

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

**High Risk — implemented reductions**

1. **Loss of gender-identity detail.**  
   Gender-identity questions were removed from the 2025 questionnaire, eliminating the ability to produce equivalent future transgender/nonbinary subgroup measures. Sexual-orientation questions remained; these are distinct measures.  
   Sources: [official 2024 documentation](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2024/srvydesc-508.pdf); [KFF analysis, December 2025](https://www.kff.org/lgbtq/trump-administration-actions-to-curb-data-collection-related-to-sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity-sogi/).

2. **Reduced temporal resolution in early-release estimates.**  
   NCHS’s May 2026 technical notes present **biannual estimates for 2025**, while quarterly estimates cover **2019–2024**. This reduces the temporal detail available in this published estimate series. It does not mean all underlying NHIS products have become semiannual.  
   Source: [Early Release technical notes](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhis/earlyrelease/earlyrelease202605-tech.pdf).

3. **Reduced annual coverage and interview-time granularity.**  
   The 2025 annual release contains 11 monthly samples. For affected October/November cases, month and quarter variables use special categories reflecting shifted collection, rather than their usual calendar detail.  
   Source: [2025 Survey Description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/srvydesc-508.pdf).

**Moderate Risk — additional proposed reductions**

- The proposed **2028 redesign** would shorten questionnaires and omit many detailed questions previously fielded annually.
- It would also abandon the current advance schedule of periodically rotating content, creating uncertainty about future availability of particular measures.
- Mixed-mode collection could introduce mode-related discontinuities, although testing and lower-cost participation could also improve coverage and sustainability.  
  Source: [August 2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-20/html/2026-17040.htm).

**No Known Issue — mitigating evidence**

- NCHS continues to publish methods, weights, codebooks, and limitations.
- The redesign retains key health measures and includes cognitive, usability, and field testing.

**Gone — not supported**

- NHIS remains operational.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Actual reductions in granularity and temporal resolution already meet the rubric. The proposed redesign adds prospective risk, but is not needed to justify this rating.

**This does not establish that all remaining NHIS estimates are inaccurate.** It establishes reduced information availability and additional comparability constraints.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

**No Known Issue — explicit mandate and established programmatic uses**

- **Public Health Service Act §306, 42 U.S.C. §242k**, provides NCHS’s statutory foundation for collecting statistics on illness, disability, and population health.
- The Federal Register describes NHIS as a leading source for the congressionally mandated **Health, United States** reporting program and a principal source for tracking HHS health objectives.
- NHIS respondents also provide the sampling frame for the **Medical Expenditure Panel Survey**, and NHIS information supports benchmarking and weight calibration for NCHS rapid surveys.  
  Sources: [NCHS legislative authorities](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/misc/legislation2014.pdf); [August 2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-20/html/2026-17040.htm).

**Moderate / High Risk — relevant limitations**

- The statute does **not freeze the NHIS questionnaire**, require every existing variable, or guarantee its present release schedule and website.
- BRFSS, NHANES, MEPS, and other collections overlap with portions of NHIS, but none is a straightforward substitute for its full population, content, design, and historical series.
- Therefore, statutory protection is strongest for the broader health-statistics mission, weaker for particular questions and dissemination practices.

**Gone — not applicable under this category**

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

NHIS has explicit statutory grounding and substantial federal programmatic use, satisfying your protective criteria. This rating is **not a guarantee against content changes, underfunding, or website relocation**.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

**High Risk — parent-agency staffing and leadership triggers**

- NPR reported in March 2026 that CDC had lost **at least one-quarter of its staff**, with broader reporting describing losses exceeding **3,000 employees**. The absolute loss exceeds your **1,000-person** High Risk threshold.
- CDC director **Susan Monarez was fired in August 2025**, meeting the rubric’s leadership-removal criterion.  
  Source: [NPR, March 25, 2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/03/25/nx-s1-5760832/cdc-turmoil-director).
- Later reporting indicates **Erica Schwartz became director in August 2026**, so the earlier vacancy should not be described as still ongoing. Nevertheless, staffing and operational recovery remained concerns.  
  Source: [Associated Press via Federal News Network, August 18, 2026](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce/2026/08/cdcs-new-director-is-pressed-to-do-something-about-its-zombie-programs/).

**Moderate Risk — NCHS-specific evidence**

- The American Statistical Association’s NCHS assessment estimates approximately **10% staffing loss by fall 2025**, meeting the Moderate Risk percentage threshold.
- It also reports terminated contracts weakening data release and publication support.
- Approximately **110 NCHS staff received October 2025 reduction-in-force notices**, but those notices were rescinded in November. These should **not** be counted as 110 permanent losses.  
  Sources: [ASA NCHS assessment](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/national-center-for-health-statistics.pdf); [AJPH commentary](https://ajph.aphapublications.org/doi/10.2105/AJPH.2026.308403).

**No Known Issue — enacted funding provides counterevidence**

- The FY2026 final appropriations analysis reports **$187.4 million for NCHS**, unchanged from FY2025.
- The administration requested **$175 million**, a proposed nominal reduction of about **6.6%**, but that request was **not the enacted amount**.
- Flat nominal funding can still lose purchasing power, but it does not establish a 10% or 20% enacted budget cut.  
  Source: [COSSA, final FY2026 appropriations analysis](https://cossa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/FY-2026-Final-LHHS-Appropriations-Analysis.pdf).

**Gone — not supported**

- Neither all staff nor all funding has been eliminated.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

CDC’s documented absolute staffing losses and removal of its director independently meet your High Risk criteria. **NCHS-specific staffing evidence alone supports Moderate Risk**, not proof that NHIS lost 40% of its staff.

## Preservation implications

**Prioritize preservation now, without treating the whole survey as already lost.**

1. Preserve original annual files **with** questionnaires, codebooks, weights, revision notices, and survey descriptions.
2. Record retrieval dates and checksums to distinguish legitimate revisions from unexplained changes.
3. Preserve the 2025 interruption documentation and older quarterly-estimate products.
4. Track OMB renewal before December 31, 2026, final 2028 specifications, and enacted funding—not just proposals.
5. Maintain independent copies of released public-use data. Such copies cannot recover withheld gender-identity records or restore missing collection coverage.

**Public-comment correction:** The official Federal Register notice gives **October 19, 2026** as the deadline for docket **CDC-2026-1387**, whereas the CDC webpage previously consulted gave October 20. Use the earlier date unless the docket confirms otherwise.
